neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert. Mood: euthymic by patient report. MoCA 21/30: executive tasks severely impaired (trails 0/1, letter fluency — 4 F-words in 1 min), memory mildly impaired (3/5 delayed recall), naming 2/3. His son reports he is 'not manic, not depressed — this is something completely different.' Notable: patient shows word-for-word repetition of a childhood story 3 times during the 20-minute visit.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Normal. Bilateral snout reflex positive. No primitive reflexes on cranial nerve exam.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone. 5/5 strength. No tremor. No rigidity. No parkinsonian features.

neurological_exam.additional: DIAGNOSTIC CHALLENGE: This patient has a 20-year history of bipolar disorder — behavioral changes in a bipolar patient can be misattributed to psychiatric disease. HOWEVER: the son correctly identifies that the current state is qualitatively different from known bipolar episodes. The perseverative repetition of the exact same story verbatim during the visit is a distinctive behavioral observation. CRITICAL: lithium toxicity causes cognitive impairment. Lithium level and renal function MUST be checked — CKD stage 2 reduces lithium clearance. Lithium level may be chronically elevated. Also: lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus is common.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive cognitive and behavioral changes in known bipolar patient — 16 months (son's report differs from patient's self-assessment)
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. E is a 66-year-old retired architect with a 20-year history of bipolar disorder type I (well-controlled on lithium for 20 years) who presents with his son for evaluation of progressive behavioral and cognitive changes. His son, who visits weekly and is familiar with his father's bipolar episodes, specifically states: 'this is NOT a mood episode — he's not manic, he's not depressed, this is different.' Over the past 16 months, his father has begun repeating verbatim the same stories from childhood in virtually every conversation — the same three anecdotes, word for word, regardless of whether they are contextually appropriate. He has lost interest in architecture and design, which defined his entire career and retirement. He no longer visits his former colleagues or attends architecture events he previously attended religiously. He has made increasingly impulsive small purchases — nothing major, but he bought 30 identical coffee mugs because they were 'on sale,' which his son found bizarre. His hygiene has declined. He has become socially withdrawn, showing little response when his grandchildren call. He does not recognize these changes in himself. The bipolar disorder has been stable — his last hospitalization was 12 years ago, and his mood has been euthymic by both patient and caregiver reports throughout this period. He has coronary artery disease (status post stenting 8 years ago) and type 2 diabetes. He has CKD stage 2 with eGFR 64. The diagnostic challenge includes: (1) behavioral change in a known bipolar patient — must exclude lithium toxicity, bipolar mixed state, or treatment-emergent effects; (2) CKD stage 2 reduces lithium clearance, creating risk for chronically elevated lithium levels; (3) vascular risk factors (CAD, diabetes) creating risk for vascular dementia; (4) the distinctive verbatim story repetition (echolalia-like perseveration) is strongly suggestive of frontotemporal pathology.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia — sporadic — in a patient with known bipolar disorder type I (lithium toxicity excluded after dose reduction and level normalization with persistent symptoms)

differential.key_features: Lithium dose reduced; level normalized to 0.9 mEq/L; behavioral syndrome UNCHANGED — confirms lithium is not the cause. Lithium toxicity at 1.28 mEq/L typically causes tremor, polyuria, confusion — not the behavioral disinhibition/perseveration pattern of FTD.

Son correctly identifies this as qualitatively different from known bipolar episodes; euthymic mood; verbatim perseveration and social withdrawal are not bipolar symptoms; MRI frontal atrophy and FDG-PET hypometabolism confirm neurodegenerative basis
Amyloid PET negative; FDG-PET frontotemporal without posterior cingulate sign; behavioral profile (perseveration, disinhibition) more typical of FTD than AD
Fazekas 1 white matter — insufficient to explain behavioral syndrome; FDG-PET metabolic changes primary, not vascular

critical_actions: Lithium level MUST be checked in any CKD patient on lithium with cognitive/behavioral changes — CKD reduces lithium clearance
Dose reduction and re-evaluation after lithium normalization is mandatory before diagnosing FTD — must exclude lithium toxicity as reversible cause first
Do NOT stop lithium abruptly — risk of bipolar rebound
contraindicated_actions: Stopping lithium abruptly without transition plan
Prescribing NSAIDs (absolute contraindication with lithium — raises lithium to toxic levels)
key_reasoning_points: Lithium toxicity must be excluded FIRST in a CKD patient on lithium with behavioral changes — however, the behavioral PROFILE is key: lithium toxicity causes tremor, ataxia, confusion; it does NOT cause the behavioral disinhibition/perseveration/social withdrawal pattern of FTD
The diagnostic sequence matters: reduce lithium dose → normalize level → reassess → if symptoms persist, proceed with neuroimaging workup
Bipolar disorder is a risk factor for cognitive impairment, but it does NOT cause FTD-pattern behavior or frontal atrophy — the co-occurrence requires FTD workup, not simply psychiatric attribution

Son's qualitative observation that current state is 'different from bipolar episodes' is a critical clinical clue — long-term observers of known psychiatric patients can reliably identify a qualitative shift

red_herrings.data_point: Lithium level 1.28 mEq/L (mildly above therapeutic range)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute entire behavioral syndrome to lithium toxicity
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mildly elevated lithium may contribute to cognitive slowing but cannot explain the behavioral FTD syndrome; after dose reduction and level normalization, symptoms unchanged — confirming FTD etiology

red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute behavioral changes to bipolar mixed state or hypomania
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The behavioral profile (perseveration, social withdrawal, disinhibition without elevated mood) is qualitatively different from known bipolar episodes; frontal atrophy on MRI and frontotemporal FDG-PET hypometabolism confirm neurodegenerative basis

metadata.notes: Moderate bvFTD in bipolar patient on lithium with CKD. Key teaching: lithium level must be checked and normalized; behavioral syndrome persists after normalization confirming FTD; behavioral profile of FTD (perseveration, social withdrawal) differs qualitatively from bipolar episode patterns.
